question: Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEIs) are ambitious, cross-border projects that support EU objectives of competitiveness, industrial policy and decarbonisation. In recent years, the use of IPCEIs has increased significantly, which can help to harness the full potential of innovative European companies and support competitiveness.

However, according to several companies across the EU, despite the lengthy and complicated procedure that is required in order to be recognised as IPCEIs, companies still face insecurity as to whether they will receive funding, because national governments often hamper access to European funds and there is no guarantee of funding actually being provided.

This uncertainty discourages European companies, endangers the continuation of innovative projects, as well as jobs connected to them, and hampers European competitiveness and innovative potential. In the light of the above-mentioned points: 1.

Is the Commission aware of these problems and if so, does it plan to adopt changes to the procedures for companies to be recognised as IPCEIs, so that companies can be guaranteed to receive European funding?
Does the Commission follow-up with the companies after they are recognised as IPCEIs and does it request information from national governments regarding the funding?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.4.2026) Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEIs) are a State aid tool enabling Member States to grant national funding to bring together knowledge, expertise and economic actors throughout the EU and create positive spillover effects to the whole EU.

The disbursement of State aid after the Commission approval decision is the sole responsibility of the respective Member State and creates neither a right nor a legally enforceable act for a beneficiary to receive the aid approved, even if named in the approval decision.

The Commission is aware that, in some approved IPCEIs, some Member States have delayed or even abandoned their initial plans to grant aid notified to and approved by the Commission, which were also identified by the European Court of Auditors1.

Aiming to prevent such potential delays, the Joint European Forum for IPCEI (JEF-IPCEI), which involves all Member States, European Economic Area countries and the Commission, agreed on and published a collection of national best practices including hands-on guidance for all national authorities when to start and how to prepare for the implementation phase of an IPCEI after the adoption of the Commission decision in an efficient manner to ensure a timely disbursal of approved aid2.

The Commission follows the implementation procedures of IPCEIs, for instance, by being ready to respond to requests from Member States and by participating in exchanges within the respective IPCEI governance body meetings. Member States involved in IPCEIs need to submit annual reports, which were standardised and streamlined in 2025 to improve efficiency.

Based, on these reports the JEF-IPCEI is developing a dashboard to monitor the implementation of IPCEIs3. For more information on aid granted by Member States, please see the State Aid Transparency website4.
